checked_sources: Explicit independent units-digit and product-length argument for all b,n
correctness.rationale: Proof independently checked by digitwise multiplication: any lunar factorization has product length len(u)+len(v)-1, so every lunar divisor has length at most len(n). All divisors are distinct positive integers at most sigma, giving d<=sigma. For n=1 the one-digit divisors are exactly 1..b-1 and equality holds; for 2<=n<=b-1 the divisor list n..b-1 is shorter than sigma=b-1. For n>=b, both n and the lunar unit b-1 divide n, so sigma has units digit b-1 and dominates the higher digits of n. If n has units digit r>0, w=n-r has zero units; if r=0, w=n+1 has unit 1. In either case w is positive, same length, <=sigma but cannot divide n since its partner would be one digit and its product units digit would be 0 or 1 instead of r. Thus w is a missing integer and d<=sigma-1 for n>1. This proves all bases without extrapolating 1019 finite tests.
residual_risks: Only ordinary comparison of positive integers is covered; no exact excess or maximal-divisor distribution.

originality.rationale: Directly answers the explicit strict lunar divisor inequality conjectured in Applegate–LeBrun–Sloane (2011) for decimal arithmetic, with a valid extension to all bases. Gross 2020 studies maximally numerous lunar divisors, not d versus sigma. No stronger already-proved statement was identified by Resultary or inspected primary paper; a later uncatalogued solution remains a historical risk.
